transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-09
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Mina Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Ravi Menon (CTO - Triad), Alison Park (Head of ML), Jordan Lee (Platform), Samir Gupta (Product)

Auto-summary (auto): quick parity mapping review and console demo, lots of questions on VPC and KMS, agreed to share sample traces and security pack.

[00:00:05] Mina: hey everyone - thanks for joining. do we have everyone on the line?
[00:00:10] Ravi: yeah, hi Mina, hi Liam, good to be here. running a little late so thanks.
[00:00:15] Alison: hi all, excited to see how we can consolidate our endpoints, we've got three different vendors right now.
[00:00:20] Mina: perfect — quick agenda: 1) understand current stack, 2) walk through parity approach (where things tend to break), 3) console + API demo mapping, 4) security and pilot next steps. sound good?
[00:00:30] Jordan: yes. also we want to talk about dedicated vs hosted - network constraints may push us to private.

[00:01:05] Liam: okay so just high level, Triad — you mentioned OpenAI, Anthropic, Together; are those segmented by use-case or model family?
[00:01:15] Samir: yeah roughly — OpenAI for chat assistants, Anthropic for long-form summarization, Together for vector embeddings in a few repos. we cobbled an adapter layer on top but it's an operational headache.
[00:01:28] Mina: makes sense. so the goal is a single Redwood-backed endpoint that can route to the appropriate model variant and preserve behavioral parity. when we say parity, what matters most — exact token-level match, or behavioral equivalence (safety, tone, latency)?
[00:01:45] Alison: behavioral equivalence + safety. we don't need token-perfect outputs but can't have hallucination regressions.
[00:01:52] Ravi: and latency envelope — we have an SLO of 350ms p95 for short chat workloads. cost is important but after latency.

[00:02:30] Liam: great — that helps prioritize. I'll sketch a mapping approach: inputs -> normalizer -> model mapping -> post-processing. normalizer handles prompt templating differences (OpenAI system prompts vs Anthropic system messages vs Together formats).
[00:02:44] Liam: side note — sometimes transcripts call our product Red wood, red wood optimize, red-wud, so bear with the auto transcribe.
[00:02:55] Alison: haha noted.

[00:03:25] Liam: demo time. I'll share my screen — first the Redwood API adapter example: we have a small node/python script that takes an OpenAI style request and rewrites it to Redwood's API. it also applies a model variant hint (e.g., 'fast-gpt' vs 'quality-gpt') and can add fallback routing.
[00:03:45] [00:03:46] Liam: (shows code) sample: 
- request from app: {model: "gpt-4o", prompt: ...} 
- adapter maps to Redwood model: "rw/gpt-4o-int8-fp16" and sets streaming true + kv_cache hint if iterative.

[00:04:20] Alison: how do you preserve temperature/stop token semantics? Together has slightly different stop-behavior.
[00:04:30] Liam: we map semantics — stop tokens are preserved, but we sometimes emulate sampling differences by adjusting temperature and top_p mapping. we add a small post-processing filter to trim or normalise whitespace. it's not magic but it gets you within behavioral parity in most cases.

[00:05:12] Samir: what about function calling? we rely on structured outputs from OpenAI — can Redwood replicate?
[00:05:20] Mina: yes — Redwood supports function-style structured output. the console shows a function schema mapping and you can pin model variants that have been validated to handle function calls reliably.

[00:06:00] Liam: next — Console tour: routing policies. you can create rules like 'latency-first' for chat (route to smaller faster quantized variants), 'quality-first' for summarization, and a fallback chain if capacity is constrained. this is important because you mentioned an SLO.
[00:06:20] [00:06:21] Liam: (shows console) here is a route: /api/chat -> policy: latency-first -> model: rw/fast-chat-8q -> fallback: rw/quality-chat-16q -> region fallback: eu-west-1.

[00:06:55] Jordan: for private deployment — we have strict egress control, can we host Redwood Private with VPC peering?
[00:07:03] Mina: absolutely — for Private we provide a customer-managed control plane and can enable VPC peering or on-prem packages if needed. we integrate with KMS/HSM for keys.
[00:07:12] Ravi: any customers with HSM deployments?
[00:07:15] Mina: yes — a couple of fintechs. we'll share the security pack with SOC2 reports and the HSM KMS integration doc.

[00:08:05] Alison: curious about the kv cache behavior. our workloads have repeated context snippets — KV caching is important to cut cost.
[00:08:13] Liam: we do prefix-based KV caching. typical pattern: you identify heavy prefixes (e.g., system+recent history) and cache the key-value layers. that reduces per-token compute and helps satisfy latency SLOs. caveat: caching is more effective for few-shot or repeated queries.

[00:09:00] Samir: can we maintain the exact prompt weighting? we use a lot of dynamic system instructions.
[00:09:10] Liam: yes the adapter preserves system messages as separate fields; in the mapping script we maintain ordering and meta flags. we can also do prompt rewriting for lower-cost variants.

[00:10:25] Mina: cost discussion — we showed an initial estimate in the deck: consolidating three vendors into Redwood usually saves on per-token overhead due to unified batching and caching. we'll run a cost parity calc off the traces you share.
[00:11:00] Alison: onboarding effort? how long to get to pilot?
[00:11:07] Mina: typical is 2-4 weeks for a small pilot: adapter script + a controlled traffic slice + eval set for quality regressions. if you need Private/OEM, add extra time for network and security reviews.

[00:13:20] [00:13:21] Liam: deep-dive: sampling semantics can diverge — for example, Together's logits may be calibrated differently. we sometimes run an auto-tuning step where we tweak temperature mapping and compare on a small eval set to find equivalence thresholds.

[00:15:40] Jordan: okay practical question — what does the rollout look like in prod? we want canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to previous vendor if Redwood pushes a bad model.
[00:15:51] Mina: console supports canary rollouts by traffic percentage; you can configure automatic rollback if error rate or a quality metric crosses a threshold. we also expose logs and traces for sampling differences so you can compare outputs side-by-side.

[00:17:05] Alison: security again — audit logs retention? compliance requires 1 year immutable logs.
[00:17:12] Mina: audit log retention is configurable and we offer enterprise packages for longer retention and append-only audit logs. we'll include options in the pack.

[00:18:30] Samir: do you have any automated eval tooling? we need to detect regressions across our prompt suite.
[00:18:39] Liam: yes, Redwood Optimize includes eval runs and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. you can run weekly jobs and get diff reports that highlight quality deltas. it's not perfect — human review is still the final gate — but it's helpful.

[00:21:00] Mina: let's try a live parity example. Liam, can you show an OpenAI chat request and how the adapter transforms it and the resulting Redwood response?
[00:21:10] Liam: sure — (runs script) here's an OpenAI style request -> adapter -> Redwood API. response time for this sample (dev env) was ~220ms on the fast variant. output looked close; there was one small tokenization difference where punctuation moved.
[00:22:00] Alison: that latency looks promising. what's the expected p95 in prod for fast variants?
[00:22:07] Liam: depends on hardware and sequence length, but we commonly hit 200-450ms p95 for fast quantized variants on dedicated pools. you'll see better numbers in-hosted vs shared dedicated setups with optimized kernels.

[00:24:10] Ravi: can you show where to configure model pinning? we sometimes need deterministic outputs for compliance.
[00:24:18] Liam: in the console -> Models -> Deployments -> you can pin model version and disable autoswap; we also support immutable snapshots for a rollout.

[00:27:35] Jordan: about private peering — any special firewall rules? our security team will want an IP allowlist and mTLS.
[00:27:43] Mina: we support IP allowlists, mTLS, and SAML SSO. detailed setup will be in the security doc but yes, it's supported.

[00:31:00] Samir: let's talk criteria for success for the pilot. we want: 1) behavior parity on top 50 prompts, 2) latency p95 under 350ms, 3) no security gaps.
[00:31:12] Mina: that's a solid set. we'll propose an eval harness and map the top 50 prompts to a quality tolerance threshold.

[00:33:45] Liam: closing the tech piece — known gotchas: function call semantics, slightly different sampling calibrations, and embeddings dimensionality differences (Together sometimes uses a different norm). we include a mapping table for typical providers.

[00:35:10] Alison: embeddings — we use Together embeddings for vector search. are there migration implications?
[00:35:18] Liam: if you want to swap embeddings you can either regenerate vectors over time or keep hybrid approach: Redwood can host Together-compatible embedding variants for a period while you backfill. we have tooling to help orchestrate incremental re-indexing.

[00:38:00] Mina: ok quick recap and next steps. we'll: 1) send security pack + SSO/KMS notes, 2) Liam will provide the adapter quick-start script and an example mapping table, 3) Triad shares one representative endpoint + traces.
[00:38:20] Ravi: sounds good. on network I'll pull Jordan & infra owner into the follow-up thread.

[00:40:00] Samir: one more question on pricing — do you have committed reserved capacity options vs usage?
[00:40:07] Mina: yes, Redwood Dedicated offers reserved GPU pools and pricing discounts for commits; hosted usage is pay-as-you-go. we'll include pricing scenarios for pilot and annual commit in the follow-up.

[00:42:15] Alison: thanks — this is helpful. two week-ish run to get artifacts together?
[00:42:22] Mina: yep target pilot kickoff week of 2026-06-22, pending artifact delivery.

[00:44:25] Alison: appreciate it.
